w: What's tested Primary vs secondary functions; muscles and ligaments position the jaw when the teeth are apart Neural control: central pattern generator, engrams, reflexes The chewing cycle: phases, 16-18 mm open and 5-6 mm lateral, return to ICP, tooth contact patterns Chewing differences: food hardness, cusp form, TMJ pain, one-sided chewing; bite force numbers and where force is highest Swallowing: what triggers it, somatic vs visceral, force and counts, the three stages Speech: no tooth contact; fricatives (f, v) and the wet-dry line; "s" and closest speaking space When we move our jaws we have limits (the border movements), but we rarely go there except the superior border. Most function happens with the teeth apart and far from the borders, which keeps it fast. "When the teeth are not in contact, mandibular position is determined by the muscles and ligaments (not anterior or condylar guidance)." Teeth only influence motion when they touch. The masticatory (stomatognathic) system has three primary functions, mastication, swallowing (deglutition) and speech, and two secondary ones, respiration and expression of emotions. Part 1: mastication The masticatory cycle is the rhythmic, well-controlled separation and closure of the teeth; all the movement is the mandible's (if your maxilla moves, "you need a surgeon"). It is the first step of digestion, so the body prioritizes it. The CNS receives afferent input from the PDL, tongue, TMJs, periosteum, muscle spindles and mucosa; the brainstem and up to the thalamus process it quickly (pleasure keeps us eating; a filled stomach inhibits it), and efferents activate some muscle groups and inhibit others. Noxious stimuli are avoided by reflexes: biting a hard surprise triggers a polysynaptic reflex that stops the closers and fires the openers at once, while a simpler myotactic reflex maintains posture. A central pattern generator times activity between antagonistic muscles and creates learned patterns called engrams. It is mostly subconscious but can be brought under conscious control, like breathing or walking, and it constantly adjusts the stroke from feedback such as particle size. Much of this came from chewing studies (Case Western's Gnathic Replicator, then the University of Florida) that are reproduced today with jaw tracking like ModJaw. The chewing stroke has an opening phase (more vertical, with a lateral slide at the end) and a closing component: the crushing phase (gradual vertical and horizontal motion that traps the bolus, closing at an angle because the posterior teeth are inclined) and then the grinding phase (a small lateral slide at the very end). Chewing opens only about 16-18 mm and moves about 5-6 mm laterally. Seen from the side on the working (food) side, the mandible opens anteriorly, then moves posteriorly in early closure, aligning the teeth with the masseter's maximum force vector. On the non-working side movement is mostly vertical, and its condyle moves more and stays anteriorly positioned during closure (the slides add that the working-side condyle is often posterior to CR during closure). Early chewing has more anterior movement (incising) and more lateral movement; both decrease as the food breaks down. Harder food means more lateral movement and more power; some patients don't change their stroke count with texture. About 78% of patients chew mostly on one side, usually the side with the most contacts in lateral glide. That loads the TMJs unequally, normally without problems because the superior lateral pterygoids stabilize the discs. Early studies predicted no tooth contact during chewing, but some does occur, and contacts return to ICP every time: "no matter how you run around the bases, you always come back to home plate." Contact increases as the bolus breaks down, to nearly every stroke before the swallow. The average contact lasts about 194 ms. Gliding contacts (cusp inclines passing each other) occur in the opening (56%) and grinding (60%) phases; single contacts occur close to MICP. Cusp form shapes the stroke: tall cusps and deep fossae promote a mostly vertical stroke; flattened cusps encourage a broader, more horizontal one. In a heavy bruxer, MIP "becomes a range... a zone," because they can close almost anywhere. Patients with TMJ pain chew with less repeatable, slower, shorter and more irregular strokes. Greatest ever measured 975 lb-force Male maximum 118-142 lb Female maximum 79-99 lb First molar 91-198 lb Incisor 29-51 lb Carrots / meat About 30 lb / about 16 lb Dentures About 25% of maximum (Dr. Givan: closer to 15%) Force drops the farther you are from the condyles: the first molar has about three to five times the force of the central incisor, which is how anterior teeth get away with off-axis loading. Bite force rises with age to maturity and with practice (tough diets); men are higher than women, though body size matters more. A high FMA (divergent jaws, long face) means lower forces; a square, low-angle face means high forces. With unilateral chewing of bread, forces on both sides are about equal. A restoration left 0.5 mm high doubles the force. With tougher foods, chewing happens mostly at the second premolar and first molar, which supports the shortened dental arch concept. Anterior slides of the teeth (a "long centric") are rarely seen in function. The tongue handles taste and sensation, divides the food, puts it back on the chewing surfaces, forms the bolus and sweeps the teeth after the swallow, "our knife, fork, and spoon." It couldn't do it without the buccinator, which forms a controlled wall and returns food from the vestibule. Part 2: swallowing Deglutition is a series of muscle contractions that moves a bolus from the mouth through the esophagus to the stomach, partly voluntary but mostly involuntary and reflex. (Gustation = tasting; olfaction = smelling; anosmic = complete loss of smell; hyposmic = reduced smell.) The not-necessarily-conscious decision to swallow depends on the fineness of the food, the intensity of taste extracted, and the lubrication of the bolus. Stabilizing the mandible is what matters most, so the hyoid can move. Adults use a somatic swallow: the teeth come together in MIP and the elevators hold the mandible there. A visceral (infantile) swallow braces the mandible by pushing the tongue forward between the arches; it is normal until the posterior teeth erupt (and when swallowing liquids), but if over-retained it displaces teeth anteriorly, e.g. an anterior open bite. Swallowing contacts are heavy and long, about 66.5 lb for about 683 ms, 7.8 lb more than chewing, and they happen in ICP, not a retruded position as once thought. We swallow about 590 times a day: 146 during meals, 394 between meals while awake (mostly saliva) and 50 asleep. 1 (voluntary) The tongue separates the food; the bolus on its dorsum is pressed lightly against the palate, tongue tip behind the incisors; lips sealed, teeth closed; a reflex wave pushes the bolus back into the pharynx Stages 1 + 2 about 1 second 2 Pharyngeal constrictor peristalsis carries the bolus to the esophagus; the soft palate rises and seals the nasal passage; the epiglottis closes over the trachea; the Eustachian tube openings open (normally closed) 3 Peristalsis carries the bolus to the cardiac sphincter, which relaxes into the stomach; the upper esophagus has some voluntary control to return food for more chewing 6-7 seconds Swallowing is studied by videofluoroscopic swallowing study, dynamic MRI and (historically) cinefluorography. For patients who can't wear dentures but struggle to swallow, a record-base-like appliance gives them something to stabilize against. Part 3: speech The diaphragm forces air from the lungs; controlled contraction and relaxation of the vocal cords sets pitch (B vs P, D vs T, G vs K differ only by voicing). The tongue, lips, cheeks and mandible shape the cavity for resonance and articulation. Most speech uses a prolonged expiration with a quick breath at a pause. After learning, speech is totally subconscious, a "learned reflex." Tooth contacts do not normally occur in speech: it is too rapid, and contact would damage teeth. Malpositioned teeth can still affect the sound. Fricatives (f, v): the maxillary incisal edge should lightly touch the wet-dry line (vermilion border) of the lower lip. Can't make the sound: incisors may be too short. Depressing the lip: too long. Clinically important when placing incisors a patient no longer has. Sibilants (s): the teeth come closest, about 1-1.5 mm apart. "Let S be your guide": the closest speaking space helps set a functional vertical dimension. M: nasopharynx open, tongue neutral, teeth apart, lips together. P and B: plosives, lips together, soft palate sealed. K and G: back of the tongue against the soft palate, anterior teeth slightly apart. T and D: tongue against the palate behind the teeth, so the cingulum contour matters. Wide-open vowels and diphthongs ("eight," "nine") separate the teeth about 5-10 mm. "In chewing and swallowing, I am amazed by the orchestration of so many different muscle groups... occurring without conscious thought, rapidly, repeatedly, and with great efficiency."
